title: Mayor names personal care home beds as the city's 2016 advocacy priority with the province
summary: Opening the first meeting of 2016, Mayor Goertzen listed advocating to the province 'specifically for PCH beds' among council's goals for the year. In October 2016 Councillor Zwaagstra said the city had already committed a city contribution toward more personal care home beds. No public report on that advocacy or on the contribution appears in the 2016–2017 transcripts.
status_detail: No council resolution, letter or delegation on personal care home beds is recorded in the 2016–2017 transcripts. The only new care-bed project council saw was a private developer's 56-bed proposal at 333 Loewen Boulevard, rezoned in 2017 (see 2017-333-loewen-care-home).
figures: Amount and terms of the city's personal care home contribution not stated in the transcripts (Zwaagstra, 2016-10-04 0:24:39).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Care beds are a provincial decision; the city's role is to advocate with the province. (Chris Goertzen)
notes: The city contribution commitment probably predates December 2015 (before the transcripts begin); its amount and status are unverified.

title: Letters from the Bethesda Foundation and health and youth charities received as information
summary: Letters from the Bethesda Foundation (Jan 2016), KidSport (Mar 2017), Youth for Christ (Nov 2017, twice), Katie Cares (Nov 2017), the Lions Club's Smart Choices program and Ronald McDonald House Charities (Dec 2017) were taken as information, mostly without discussion. Councillor Fehr praised the Bethesda Foundation in an opening for advocating for health-care funding for the region.
status_detail: No grants decided in public; some were taken as information 'for now', possibly for budget time. The 2017 grants list (accepted in 2018) shows small grants of $200–$350 to groups such as Youth for Christ, KidSport and the Eden Foundation.
figures: 2017 small grants $200–$350 each (minutes R18-065, per data/taxes-spending/raw/2017-2018.json).
reasons: fairness-precedent: The city is 'typically not interested in providing operating grants' (Dec 5, 2017). (John Fehr)
public: Content and amounts of the letters were not read aloud.
notes: Katie Cares and Ronald McDonald House Charities are children's health charities; what they asked of the city is not stated.

title: Residents' request for a sidewalk with the Old Tom Road paving deferred to the sidewalk plan
summary: Residents asked for a sidewalk along Old Tom Road as part of its paving. Staff said a sidewalk could cost $700,000–$800,000, about as much as the paving. Councillors agreed not to tie it to the paving and to consider it later in the overall sidewalk plan; Councillor Siemens pointed to the city's pathway work toward Deerfield and the mayor to future regional pathways after annexation.
status_detail: Letter received; no sidewalk added to the 2016 paving and no later decision found in 2016–2017.
figures: Sidewalk $700,000–$800,000 (residents' estimate as reported by the city manager, 1:19:50); $1M set aside for the paving project.
reasons: cost: It would virtually double the paving budget. (John Fehr (probable; diarization unclear)); study-first: Consider it within the overall sidewalk plan rather than with paving. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Mr. and Mrs. T. (Lyons Gate residents) wrote asking for the sidewalk.
notes: Also in data/advocacy/raw/2015-2016.json.

title: Recreation in the 2016 and 2017 financial plans: subsidized aquatic centre, a pool reserve and planned upgrades
summary: The city's financial plans described subsidized user fees so programs like the aquatic centre and arena stay accessible; the aquatic centre used about 20% of all city staff hours, the largest of any department. Council put $100,000 of the 2016 surplus into the pool reserve for coming capital work, and in July 2017 the mayor said the 2018 capital plan included aquatic centre upgrades.
status_detail: 2016 plan approved Feb 16, 2016; 2017 plan approved in principle Feb 21, 2017 (Zwaagstra and Funk against over the performing arts centre); pool reserve transfer approved Mar 7, 2017. The 2018 upgrades belong to the next period.
figures: Aquatic centre about 20% of city labour hours (2016 and 2017 plans); recreation facilities operating and maintenance $3.4M in 2017 (2017-02-21 hearing 0:00:49); aquatic centre about $1.6M operating cost and about $800,000 net deficit (mayor, 2017-06-20 0:07:36); $100,000 to the pool reserve from the 2016 surplus (2017-03-07 0:08:36).
reasons: regional-users: Most aquatic centre users live outside Steinbach while Steinbach taxpayers cover its deficit (see 2016-recreation-regional-users). (Councillor Penner (probably Susan Penner))
public: No members of the public spoke at either financial plan hearing.
mover: 2016 plan: Michael Zwaagstra; 2017 plan: a Councillor Penner; pool reserve: a Councillor Penner
seconder: 2017 plan: John Fehr; pool reserve: Earl Funk
vote: 2016 plan carried (no dissent stated); 2017 plan carried with Zwaagstra and Funk stating they would vote against; reserve transfer carried
notes: The 2016 recreation operating figure was cut off in the transcript.

title: Washroom and change-room building finally added at the Steinbach Soccer Park
summary: Council authorized about $370,000 for a washroom and change-room building at the soccer park, which had relied on portable toilets for about 10 years, in time for the 2016 Manitoba Summer Games. The province's Community Places program later contributed $35,000.
status_detail: Expenditure approved Mar 15, 2016; reported complete with a $35,000 Community Places grant on Aug 2, 2016.
figures: About $370,000 (city manager, 2016-03-15 0:08:27); $35,000 Community Places grant (mayor, 2016-08-02 0:20:14).

title: Canadian Blood Services asks council to champion Steinbach's donor clinic
summary: Canadian Blood Services' territory manager told council Steinbach's community clinic was the largest it runs in Manitoba and was moving to every two weeks, needing about 750 new and active donors. He asked councillors to promote the clinic through their networks and cited the RM of Gimli's supporting resolution and mayors who greet donors. Council asked no questions; the mayor said the information would go to staff.
status_detail: Information passed to staff; no resolution or council pledge like Gimli's.
figures: 1,572 units collected that clinic year; biweekly clinics with a goal of 96 units each; about 750 new and active donors needed (delegate S.R., 0:11:22).
public: S.R. (Canadian Blood Services) made the request.

title: Headway at-risk youth program asks the city for funding
summary: Headway, a new multi-agency wraparound program for at-risk youth and their families (RCMP, Child and Family Services, Hanover School Division, Mental Health, the Addictions Foundation), asked the city to help close a $20,000 gap; the RCMP staff sergeant backed it. The mayor promised a reply under the city's grant policy. A follow-up funding letter (June 2016) and an RCMP letter on Headway funding (November 2017) were both received as information.
status_detail: No grant decision appears in the 2016–2017 transcripts; both written requests were received as information without discussion.
figures: About $20,000 still sought (delegate B.B., 2016-04-05 part 2, 0:01:04 / 0:09:19).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Request to be answered under the city's grant policy and guidelines rather than on the spot. (Chris Goertzen)
public: B.B., Headway coordinator, said the program refers youth to mental health and addictions services and cited results elsewhere (her claims, unverified). RCMP Staff Sgt. H.L. said the program would not exist without the city's support and asked for continued help.
notes: Also recorded in data/crime-policing/raw/2015-2017.json. Whether the city ever funded Headway is not shown in 2015–2017.

title: Council drops the multiplex and adopts principles for future recreation facilities
summary: After years of studies, a Councillor Penner moved and Councillor Zwaagstra seconded five principles: a multiplex is not financially feasible; plan a downtown performing arts centre only with parking, other-government money and 10% private fundraising; look for land for a future spectator arena outside downtown; and keep putting 1.241 mills a year into the recreation reserve. Supporters said the reserve would still fund 'small high-impact projects' such as the splash park and Bush Farm pathway. Mayor Goertzen opposed it as abandoning the master plan just as federal infrastructure money was opening up.
status_detail: Carried; the video ends during debate, before the vote. Other topic files record 5-2 (Goertzen and Fehr against) from SteinbachOnline; not verified here. No arena land purchase followed in 2016–2017, and the performing arts centre was dropped in July 2017 after missing its funding deadline.
figures: Multiplex estimates over $100M (MNP 2012) and about $71M (Stantec); city tax revenue about $13M a year; recreation reserve 1.241 mills, about $1.1M a year (transcript 2016-04-05 part 2, 0:46:46, 0:50:47).
reasons: cost: A city taking in $13M a year cannot afford a $71M–$100M multiplex without massive tax increases. (Councillor Penner (mover)); partner-money: Two-thirds funding from other governments is unrealistic, and even then borrowing would force a tax increase. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The task force's public survey (Mar 15, 2016) favoured a downtown arts centre but raised parking concerns.
mover: Councillor Penner (Susan Penner per SteinbachOnline; not confirmed on the audio)
vote: carried; 5-2 (against: Goertzen, Fehr) per SteinbachOnline, not on the recording
decision_source: transcript (motion and debate); vote count from news report via other topic files
notes: Fuller record in data/future-planning/raw/2015-2016.json and data/taxes-spending/raw/2015-2016.json.

title: Neighbourhood playground renewals with provincial Community Places grants
summary: The city renewed older neighbourhood parks on a rolling list (Southwood, Poplar Park in 2016, Chote Park in 2017), applying to the province's Community Places program each time. Council approved the Chote Park application in September 2017 and the grant of up to $10,557 was reported in November.
status_detail: Chote Park application approved Sep 5, 2017; grant of up to $10,557 received as information Nov 21, 2017. Poplar Park's Community Places letter received Aug 2, 2016.
figures: Community Places grant up to $10,557 for Chote Park (Zwaagstra, 2017-11-21 0:32:59).
public: Chote Park neighbours held a fundraising party to enhance their renewed playground (reported by a councillor, May 17, 2016).

title: Renewing the city's grant program for assisted-living and supportive seniors housing
summary: In May 2016 Mayor Goertzen asked council whether to renew the city's earlier seniors housing grant program, which had run twice and drawn applications; council agreed he would work with administration on it for the budget. In October, when the Haven Group asked for a development-fee rebate for 55+ housing, the city manager explained the old program only funded assisted-living or supportive housing confirmed by Southern Health, and Councillor Zwaagstra argued city money should stay targeted at care beds and supportive housing.
status_detail: Council agreed to write to the Haven Group with the old program's criteria and ask whether its project included supportive or assisted living; no renewed program and no rebate decision appear in the 2016–2017 transcripts.
reasons: targeted-only: Grants should go to personal care home beds, assisted living and supportive care, not regular 55+ housing. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Funding regular 55+ housing would open a new category that much other housing could claim. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The Haven Group (a seniors housing organization) asked by letter for a development-fee rebate for its 55+ project.
vote: consensus (no motion): mayor to work with administration (May 17); write back to the Haven Group (Oct 4)
notes: When the original program ran and how much it paid are not stated in the 2015–2017 transcripts.

title: Seniors housing rezonings approved near the new primary health care centre and Woodhaven Manor
summary: Council rezoned land beside the Bridge Park seniors campus on Stonebridge Crossing (a non-profit whose mission is 'independent healthy living for seniors') for future seniors housing, and rezoned Woodhaven Avenue/Brant Street land for the Haven Group's 61-unit seniors building beside Woodhaven Manor. Councillors repeatedly said Steinbach urgently needs more seniors housing; one noted the Bridge Park site is close to the new primary health care centre.
status_detail: Bridge Park: first reading Jun 21, second reading Jul 19, 2016, third reading Feb 7, 2017 after a Municipal Board referral. Haven Group: first reading Sep 6, second and third reading Oct 18, 2016, with conditions (fence, access off Woodhaven).
figures: Haven Group project about 61 units (city manager, 2016-10-18).
public: An Albert Street neighbour (D.W.) objected to the Bridge Park rezoning without a site plan but said he was not against seniors housing; a Woodhaven neighbour raised light, traffic and property values. L.K. spoke for Bridge Park.
mover: Bridge Park 2nd reading: Michael Zwaagstra; Haven 2nd reading: Jac Siemens
seconder: Bridge Park 2nd reading: a Councillor Penner; Haven 2nd reading: John Fehr
vote: carried at each reading (no dissent stated)
notes: Detailed planning record is in data/housing-development/raw/2015-2016.json. Kept here only for the seniors and health-access angle.

title: Fly-In Golf Club: 'health and well-being' pitch, refused grant, then a $500,000 land purchase
summary: In July 2016 the Steinbach Fly-In Golf Club asked for help with water flowing through the course, compensation and a $50,000 yearly recreation grant, pitching golf as a health and wellness activity; the mayor agreed the course is 'important for people's health' and sent the asks to the budget process. Council later refused a $500,000 grant in closed session, then in December 2017 voted to buy 40 acres of the course for $500,000 over three years and lease it back for $1 a year.
status_detail: The yearly grant and the $500,000 grant were refused; the club instead got $500,000 through the land purchase and $1/year leaseback, approved Dec 5, 2017. The water-management asks had no public decision.
figures: $50,000 yearly grant asked (2016); $500,000 purchase of 40 acres paid over 3 years, leased back at $1 a year (2017-12-05, 0:58:52 onward).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Council declined the grant because it does not usually give operating grants; argued the land is an asset. (John Fehr); fairness-precedent: A bailout that is unfair to other businesses; same amount as the refused grant, no appraisal. (Earl Funk)
public: A Fly-In Golf Club board representative (Mr. S.) presented the 2016 request, citing 8,000–10,000 steps a round, about 1,000 students a year and the club's economic value.
vote: carried; count not announced. Stated positions: against Zwaagstra, Funk and one Councillor Penner; for Fehr, Siemens, Goertzen and the other Councillor Penner (implies 4-3). Lease carried; Zwaagstra said he would vote against.
notes: The club representative's first initial is unclear in the transcript, so he is shown as 'Mr. S.'. The tally of the December 2017 vote is not announced on the recording; the 4-3 split is inferred from stated positions. Full record in data/advocacy and data/taxes-spending raw files.

title: Council welcomes a Mental Health Act change that frees police from hospital waits
summary: A Councillor Penner reported that Steinbach MLA and Health Minister Kelvin Goertzen had amended Manitoba's Mental Health Act so someone other than a police officer can stay with a person waiting for a mental health assessment at hospital. The issue had been raised years earlier by the city's RCMP Advisory Group with the local staff sergeant, who found officers waiting hours at the hospital.
status_detail: The amendment passed the Legislature (as reported to council); council recorded its thanks. No later report on the effect in Steinbach appears in 2016–2017.
notes: Which Councillor Penner spoke is not determinable; an RCMP officer said in April 2016 that both Penners helped through the RCMP Advisory Committee.

title: Council reaffirms opposition to Manitoba's cosmetic pesticide ban, citing Health Canada and cost
summary: When the province announced a review of its ban on cosmetic pesticides, Councillor Zwaagstra moved that the city reaffirm its opposition and send the information to the province. He argued Health Canada already regulates pesticides, that municipalities and homeowners should choose, and that organic products would raise city lawn care from $18,000 to over $200,000 a year.
status_detail: Motion carried (no dissent stated); the mayor said it would be submitted to the province.
figures: Lawn care with organic products over $200,000 a year vs $18,000; extra mowing policy $30,000–$40,000 a year (Zwaagstra, 1:14:52).
reasons: cost: The ban raises city lawn-care costs and leaves more weeds on sports fields. (Michael Zwaagstra); not-council-role: Health Canada, not the province, should regulate pesticide safety; use should be a local and personal choice. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Included as a healthy-environment item; Manitoba's ban was framed by the province as a health and environment measure (not discussed at council).

title: Who pays for regional recreation: councillor says non-residents use the aquatic centre while Steinbach covers its deficit
summary: In opening remarks, a Councillor Penner said the majority of aquatic centre users do not live in Steinbach but Steinbach residents cover its 'significant operating deficit', and the same would happen with a performing arts centre. She asked whether the city could partner with surrounding RMs on regional facilities to attract more provincial and federal grants.
status_detail: No regional cost-sharing agreement for recreation facilities was brought to council in 2016–2017.
reasons: regional-users: Most aquatic centre users are non-residents; Steinbach taxpayers carry the deficit. (Councillor Penner (probably Susan Penner))
notes: No user-residency data was presented to support the 'majority' claim.

title: Sign approvals for the Bethesda Regional Health Centre and the new Stonebridge medical centre
summary: Council approved a variance letting Bethesda Regional Health Centre place directional signs at its property line, one by the emergency entrance (Nov 2016), and conditional uses for electronic signs for Bethesda Wellness Inc.'s medical centre at 380 Stonebridge Crossing and a related lot (Aug 2017), so patients could find a centre that is off the main roads.
status_detail: Variance V-2016-17 carried Nov 15, 2016; CU-2017-03 and CU-2017-04 carried Aug 1, 2017 (no objections).
public: No objections were filed.
mover: V-2016-17: a Councillor Penner; CU-2017-03: Earl Funk or Michael Zwaagstra (order unclear on the audio); CU-2017-04: Earl Funk
seconder: V-2016-17: Earl Funk; CU-2017-03: the other of Funk/Zwaagstra; CU-2017-04: Jac Siemens
notes: The primary health care centre on Stonebridge Crossing is mentioned as 'new' in July and October 2016; its opening date is not given in the transcripts.

title: Parking variance denied for extra suites meant partly for Eden Health mental-health clients
summary: A builder asked to put 22 suites instead of 15 in a second building at 295 Loewen Boulevard with fewer parking stalls than required, saying Eden Health (a mental-health program of the Mennonite churches) wanted one-bedroom suites, faced a shortage of suitable housing in Steinbach, and that few of its clients drive. Administration recommended denial and neighbours objected to street parking; council denied the variance.
status_detail: Motion to deny carried (no dissent stated); the 22-suite version did not proceed.
figures: 22 suites with 26 stalls vs 36 required; rule 1.5 stalls per unit plus 10% visitor parking (Zwaagstra, 0:22:06).
reasons: parking-rules: No long-term guarantee future tenants would need less parking. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: L.S., for the builder, described Eden Health's shortage of suitable suites. Neighbours objected to street parking and traffic.
vote: carried (motion to deny; no dissent stated)
notes: Detail in data/housing-development/raw/2015-2016.json.

title: Aquatic Centre opened on Louis Riel Day and Victoria Day
summary: The day after Family Day 2017, a Councillor Penner asked why the pool closes on statutory holidays when families are off; council asked staff for a report on usage and costs. Staff found high public interest, and in June council voted to open on Louis Riel Day and Victoria Day and close on Remembrance Day, a net one extra day.
status_detail: Motion carried Jun 20, 2017 (no dissent heard).
figures: Aquatic centre about $1.6M operating cost, about $800,000 net deficit (mayor, 2017-06-20 0:07:36).
reasons: cost: Recreation facilities always carry financial implications; staff recommended only the two highest-interest holidays. (Troy Warkentin)
public: Staff's informal surveys showed 'very high interest'; a councillor cited families on Facebook looking for things to do on Family Day.
notes: Also in data/advocacy/raw/2017.json.

title: City asks Manitoba Health whether new mosquito research changes its larviciding program
summary: Councillor Zwaagstra cited a CBC report that many Culex mosquitoes lay eggs beside water rather than on it and asked whether the city's larviciding was still effective; council agreed to pass the question to the province. Staff reported that Manitoba Health, which directs the city's program, saw no need to change it.
status_detail: Question sent to Manitoba Health; reply reported May 2, 2017: no change to the 2017 program.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Manitoba Health sets the parameters, methods and standards the city's larviciding follows. (Troy Warkentin)
notes: The transcripts refer to the 'common nuisance mosquito'; West Nile virus was not mentioned.

title: Rezoning for a private 56-bed care home with supportive living at 333 Loewen Boulevard
summary: A private developer proposed a 9-storey 'continuing care retirement community' on the old clinic site at 333 Loewen Boulevard: 56 personal care (long-term care) beds, 56 supportive living units and 33 seniors' apartments. Its architect told council the province had suspended all personal care home projects and that the apartments were needed to make privately built care beds pay. Council rezoned the site to residential mixed use (its first use) and approved a 120-foot height.
status_detail: First reading Jun 6; second reading Jul 18, 2017 (R17-141, unanimous); third reading and height variance V-2017-13 carried Aug 15, 2017 after the last objector withdrew. Whether the care home was built (it depended on provincial care-bed funding) is not shown in this period.
figures: 56 long-term care beds, 56 supportive living, 33 apartments; 120 ft vs 85 ft RMX limit (transcript 2017-07-18 0:11:22, 0:34:39); 'A personal care bed costs $450,000' and a provincial goal of 1,800 beds (architect R.R., 0:41:15).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: No care homes were being built because the province lacked the money; the private model needs extra revenue from apartments. (R.R. (applicant's architect))
public: Neighbours objected mainly to the building's height and to traffic and sidewalk safety on Albert Street; the last written objection was withdrawn before third reading. R.R. (MMP Architects) presented for the developer.
decision_source: minutes 2017-07-18 (R17-141); third reading and variance Aug 15 from transcript (moved and seconded by the two Councillors Penner, which is which not shown)
notes: Planning detail also in data/housing-development/raw/2017-2018.json.

title: Letter against federal small-business tax changes cites doctor recruitment
summary: A Councillor Penner moved, and Councillor Zwaagstra seconded, a letter asking Ottawa to abandon proposed changes to how small corporations are taxed. In support, a councillor (probably Zwaagstra) said council had 'talked a lot about doctor recruitment' and did not want rules that make it harder for incorporated doctors to recover their medical-school costs. It is the only mention of physician recruitment in the 2015–2017 transcripts.
status_detail: Motion carried; letter sent. On Nov 7, 2017 council received the Finance Minister's reply as information, noting Ottawa had since moderated some changes.
public: The Steinbach Chamber of Commerce had asked the city to support its own letter.
notes: No physician-recruitment program, committee or budget line is discussed in public in 2015–2017; 'we've talked a lot about doctor recruitment' may refer to earlier years or closed sessions.

title: Eden Health Care Services describes Steinbach's mental-health housing and drop-in programs
summary: At council's invitation, Eden Foundation and Eden Health Care Services described their Steinbach programs: 48 subsidized or affordable suites begun because people with mental health issues could not find housing, a weekday drop-in (Positive Living), a wellness library, a youth job program, and psychiatrist consultation to Southern Health's mental health programs. The longest waitlist was single adults needing one-bedroom suites; a Steinbach building proposal to Manitoba Housing had been shelved. Council asked questions and took no action.
status_detail: Received as information; no city follow-up (land, money or advocacy) appears in 2017.
figures: 24 suites at Penfield Court and 24 at Wilson Courts; about 30 regular drop-in participants; 6–10 open housing-search files at a time (delegate B.D., 0:17:46).
public: B.D., program director of Eden's Housing and Supports Program, and an Eden Foundation representative presented.
notes: The Eden Foundation speaker's name is unclear in the transcript, so no initials are given for him.

title: Resident letter: narrow Henry Street by the hospital is treacherous
summary: A resident wrote that Henry Street beside Bethesda hospital feels too narrow and is dangerous, especially in winter. Staff said it is standard width and widening would need extensive study; councillors agreed it is uncomfortable and suggested a one-way street or widening when it is rebuilt. Council took the letter as information 'for now'.
status_detail: Received as information; no study or change ordered in 2017.
figures: 60-foot road allowance; 29-foot road surface (city manager, 1:38:18).
reasons: cost: 'it will be costly to widen the street' (Chris Goertzen); study-first: Widening would need intensive evaluation of implications and costs. (Troy Warkentin)
public: A resident's letter (initials uncertain in the transcript) described the street as tight and treacherous with hospital traffic.
notes: Also in data/advocacy/raw/2017.json.

title: Seniors' centre asks for a yearly grant in lieu of property taxes; not funded in the 2018 budget
summary: Serving Seniors Inc. (Pat Porter Active Living Centre) told council in Feb 2018 that its programs (fitness, foot care, Meals on Wheels, health education) keep older adults healthy, that Southern Health covers only 24% of operating costs, and asked for a yearly grant equal to its property taxes. Mayor Goertzen cited council's 'simplified and focused' grants policy; at the March 2018 budget hearing administration confirmed no change to grants, so the request was not funded. Councillors Funk and Siemens raised the unmet seniors' request when the 2018 budget was debated.
status_detail: No grant in lieu of taxes was approved in 2018–2020. Later support was smaller and different: an Aug 2020 letter thanked council for a stage-lighting replacement grant, the 2020–21 grants summary (R22-066, approved Mar 2022) lists Serving Seniors at $10,000 and $500 for the two years, and in Nov 2020 council agreed the mayor would write a letter supporting the centre's application to Southern Health for annual funding.
figures: Property taxes $33,600 over 3 years; operating deficits $38,572 over 3 years; must fundraise over $200,000 a year; 270 members, ~11,000 attendances in 1,700 program events; 24% of operating costs from Southern Health (delegation, 2018-02-20 transcript 0:23:30–0:26:01; minutes item 14). Serving Seniors 2020/2021 grants $10,000 and $500 (2022-03-15 minutes R22-066; column order in the extracted text is unclear).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Council has a longstanding, 'simplified and focused' policy of granting to select organizations only; no policy change, so nothing in the 2018 budget. (Chris Goertzen); targeted-only: Grants policy limited to a few core organizations (library, Chamber, Arts Council, museum). (Chris Goertzen)
public: D.E. (president) and another Serving Seniors presenter argued that the 'grants to select organizations only' policy 'shows favoritism' and that senior programs ease the burden on 'limited health resources'. L.M. returned to the March 20 budget hearing to ask why the centre had not been told of a decision.
vote: not recorded (received as information; not included in 2018 Financial Plan R18-056)
decision_source: minutes 2018-02-20 item 14; 2018-03-20 financial plan hearing minutes 4.6–4.7
notes: Speaker I's name is not given in the transcript or minutes; treated as an unnamed delegate. Whether the 2020 Serving Seniors $10,000 was the stage-lighting grant is not confirmed; the decision was not made at a recorded meeting.

title: STARS air ambulance asks for a $1-per-resident annual pledge; no decision recorded
summary: STARS told council in May 2018 that it had flown to Steinbach 24 times in the past year and asked the city to join about 40 Manitoba municipalities with an annual pledge from its protective-services budget (about a dozen give $1 per resident). Mayor Goertzen praised the service. Requests relayed by the RM of Ste. Anne (Feb 2018, Feb 2019, Feb 2020) and fundraiser invitations were all received as information.
status_detail: No pledge was approved in 2018 or 2019; the 2017–2019 grant summaries list no STARS grant. STARS returned in Sept 2020 (see 2020-stars-annual-contribution).
figures: 24 Steinbach missions in the past year; ~40 municipal partners, about a dozen at $1 per capita; Manitoba STARS budget ~89% provincial, 11% foundation (2018-05-01 transcript 0:58:01, 1:03:06, 1:08:23; minutes item 10).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Councillor questions focused on STARS being 89% provincially funded; no member argued for a pledge on the record. (council (implicit))
public: STARS representatives M.K. and G.T. presented; the RM of Ste. Anne sent letters seeking municipal support.
notes: Whether a STARS grant was discussed at an unrecorded study session in 2018–2019 is unknown.

title: Pathway network grows: Park Hill connector in the 2018 budget and the Deerfield pathway in 2019
summary: The 2018 budget put about $125,000 of new tax revenue toward a $250,000 connector pathway to the Park Hill subdivision, and in 2019 council awarded the Deerfield detention pond and pathway project for $588,550, about $120,000 under budget. Councillor Siemens repeatedly pushed for more pathways and bike paths.
status_detail: 2018 Financial Plan adopted (R18-056, 4-3, split on the golf-course purchase); Deerfield tender awarded unanimously (R19-064).
figures: Park Hill connector $250,000, ~$125,000 from new tax revenue (Siemens, 2018-03-20 financial plan hearing 0:18:11); Deerfield $588,550 + GST, low of 7 bids (R19-064).
vote: R18-056 4-3 (against: Zwaagstra, S. Penner, Funk — over the golf course purchase); R19-064 unanimous

title: Rest Haven care-home expansion (142 beds) gets its setback variance, against staff advice
summary: Rest Haven Nursing Home and Southern Health planned 142 new personal-care beds in a three-storey addition and needed an 11.5-foot front setback where 25 feet is required. Administration recommended denial; a neighbour objected to the setback while welcoming the beds. Council approved the variance unanimously, saying care-home beds had been sought for years.
status_detail: Variance V-2018-05 approved subject to a development agreement (R18-069). In Oct 2019 Mayor Funk described the PCH (143 beds, a little over $30 million) as announced that year with city and Bethesda Foundation support.
figures: 142 new beds in four 'small houses' of 12 residents (applicant, 2018-04-03 transcript 0:10:58; minutes 10.4); setback 11'6" vs 25' required.
public: T.M., a neighbour, supported the expansion but objected to the reduced setback as breaking neighbourhood standards.

title: Council puts a cannabis retail-sales question on the Oct 2018 election ballot
summary: Ahead of legalization, an April 2018 opening remark weighed a plebiscite and restrictive zoning for cannabis stores. On July 17, 2018 the mayor added a 'cannabis plebiscite' item to the agenda; on Aug 7 councillors referred to the cannabis question already going on the Oct 24, 2018 ballot (worded by the province) when they rejected a second, Sunday-shopping referendum.
status_detail: The cannabis question was on the Oct 24, 2018 ballot (councillors' remarks, 2018-08-07). The vote on July 17 is not in the record: the transcript ends at 2:00:11 before item 9F and no July 17 minutes were found. The plebiscite result is not in the council sources searched.
reasons: residents-decide: Put the question to the public to learn whether cannabis should be sold in Steinbach. (Jac Siemens)
notes: Framed in council mainly as public opinion, zoning and policing, not health. Outcome of the plebiscite not verified from council records.

title: Aquatic Centre renewal: grant applications, then a $1.48M renovation done while COVID closed the pool
summary: Council applied for a $50,000 Community Places grant (2018), a $25,722 Building Sustainable Communities study grant (2019) and federal-provincial ICIP funding toward a $2.735M multi-year renovation (2019). With the pool closed from mid-March 2020 by COVID-19 rules and reopening limited to 50% capacity, council moved the planned 2021 renovation (lighting, acoustic panels, painting) up to summer 2020 and awarded a $1.28M tender, funded from the recreation reserve.
status_detail: Tender awarded to Ernst Hansch Construction, total project budget $1,479,415 from the Recreation Reserve (R20-118, unanimous); work expected June–Aug 2020 with reopening about Sept 14, 2020. Whether the ICIP grant was received is not stated in the meetings searched.
reasons: cost: Do repairs while COVID limits capacity anyway, to avoid closing the pool in summer 2021. (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: Use every grant program available to maintain a pool heavily used by the region. (Earl Funk); regional-users: The pool is 'heavily used by our region'. (Earl Funk)

title: Health charities and youth-sport groups heard; requests received as information
summary: Canadian Blood Services (May 2019) asked council to promote blood donation and encourage staff to donate; Ronald McDonald House Charities Manitoba (Mar 2020) described a $20M+ expansion that served 88 Steinbach-area families in 2019 and invited council to share the campaign. KidSport grant requests (2018, 2019), Safe Families Steinbach (2020), and the Ste. Anne Hospital Health Walk (2020) were also received as information.
status_detail: All received as information; no motion. KidSport later appears in the 2019 grants summary at $300.
figures: CBS: 350 new Steinbach donors needed in 2019; 97.12% of local goals met (2019-05-07 minutes 7.2). RMHC: campaign over $20M, 45% raised; 88 Steinbach-area families in 2019 (2020-03-17 minutes 16).
public: S.R. (Canadian Blood Services) and W.G./T.B. (RMHC Manitoba) presented.

title: Clearspring Greens pathway: residents' safety request leads to a divided cost-sharing fight
summary: Clearspring Greens had no safe walking or cycling route to schools, the pool and A.D. Penner Park. After a 2018 letter (sent to study session) and a 2019 delegation of about 100 residents, council bought a lot at 42 Carleton Drive ($115,982.50) for the route. The Jan 2020 local-improvement bylaw for an 850 m lit asphalt path ($625,000) would have charged 146 homes $4,280.82 each; Councillors Siemens and Jake Hiebert lost a bid to cut it to unlit limestone, and two weeks later council moved the $208,000 lighting cost to city reserves.
status_detail: By-Law 2132 got first and second readings (5-2) and the lighting change passed 6-1, but the project did not proceed in 2020 (32 objections could send it to the Municipal Board; the April 2020 tender excluded it). It was redone as By-Law 2168 and tendered in April 2021 (R21-076/077, unanimous), with debenture By-Law 2195 in 2021–22.
figures: Lot $115,982.50 (R19-194); project $625,000, 146 properties at $4,280.82 up front or $1,044.05/yr for 5 years (2020-01-07 minutes 6.2–6.3); lighting $208,000 moved to Capital Development Reserve, per-home cost ~ $4,300 to ~$2,800 (2020-01-21 0:07:01); 32 objections (0:14:30).
reasons: cost: Not in favour of raising what everyone else pays for a neighbourhood path. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: A connector serving mainly the neighbourhood, not a regional trail, so the neighbourhood pays most (80/20). (Damian Penner); fairness-precedent: First time residents asked to pay most of a pathway connecting them to the city. (Jac Siemens)
public: M.F. led a delegation of about 100 residents (2019-07-16) citing unsafe roads for children walking and biking; at the Jan 7, 2020 hearing many residents objected to the cost while others wanted the lighting for safety.
mover: Damian Penner (bylaw); Jac Siemens (amendment); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-012)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (bylaw); Jake Hiebert (amendment); Damian Penner (R20-012)
vote: amendment defeated 2-5; 1st/2nd reading 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert); R20-012 6-1 (against: Siemens)

title: Hospital Street lots rezoned for the Bethesda hospital and care-home campus
summary: Southern Health asked to rezone 409, 415 and 421 Hospital Street from residential to Educational/Institutional so lots used for hospital offices (and a planned garage) conform with the Bethesda campus. After a public hearing where two neighbours raised drainage, privacy and safety concerns, council gave second and third readings unanimously, subject to consolidating the lots.
status_detail: By-Law 2109 passed (R19-045, R19-046); first reading was redone Jan 15, 2019 (R19-015) after a file error.
public: O.M. and C.K., Hospital Street neighbours, raised drainage, privacy, through-access and teenagers using the lot (2019-03-05 minutes 6.4–6.5; no transcript for that date).
notes: 2019-03-05 hearing has no transcript (not in the transcript set); minutes used.

title: Public swim fees raised for the first time in 10 years to cut the pool's deficit
summary: On a Strategic Priorities Committee recommendation, council raised public-swim admission from April 1, 2019: adults $6.50 to $7.50, seniors $6.50 to $7.00, children 3–7 from free to $5.00, youth unchanged at $6.50. Councillor Damian Penner said the pool ran a deficit over $800,000 a year and recovered about 58% of costs against a 66% target.
status_detail: R19-022 carried unanimously; fees effective April 1, 2019. The mayor expected about $80,000 a year in added revenue.
figures: Fees incl. GST: adult $7.50, youth $6.50, child $5.00, senior $7.00 (minutes R19-022); deficit >$800,000/yr, cost recovery ~58% vs 66% target (2019-02-05 0:11:31); ~$80,000 added revenue (0:13:32).
reasons: cost: Deficit over $800,000 a year; bring cost recovery back toward 66%. (Damian Penner); user-pay: Users should pay more; taxpayers still cover a large share; fees last raised in 2008. (Susan Penner (probable))
notes: No discussion of the effect on low-income families, seniors or children was recorded; a separate residency-based fee for swimming lessons was said to be under review.

title: Parent's request for pool and hot-tub lifts for a child with cerebral palsy referred to staff
summary: C.K.B. wrote that the indoor pool has a lift but the outdoor pool and hot tub do not. Councillor Zwaagstra said accessibility should be part of the ongoing pool upgrades; council agreed by consensus to have administration report back with options.
status_detail: Consensus to refer to administration (minutes 13.1). No report back or accessibility item was found in later 2019–2021 transcripts searched.
reasons: study-first: Referred to staff for options and possible grants. (council (consensus))
public: C.K.B. (parent) asked for lifts at the outdoor pool and hot tub.

title: City pledges $2 million over 7 years to the Bethesda Foundation for health projects
summary: The 2018 grants summary included a large grant to the Bethesda Foundation (Councillor Susan Penner: $900,000), tied to the new personal care home and primary health care centre; $250,000 followed in 2019 and again in 2020. Mayor Funk described the commitment as $2 million over 7 years to health-care projects, including the 143-bed PCH announced in 2019.
status_detail: 2018 grants accepted (R19-073), 2019 grants accepted (R20-064), 2020 grants accepted in Mar 2022 (R22-066) — all unanimous. Reserve transfers for 2018 included $200,000 to a committed reserve for the 'Bethesda Wellness facility' and $600,000 'Bethesda Wellness contribution' (R19-074). When the $2M pledge itself was approved is not in the meetings searched.
figures: Bethesda Foundation: 2018 $900,000 per S. Penner (minutes text shows 500,000.00, but the listed subtotal $1,232,568.21 only adds up with $900,000); 2019 $250,000 (R20-064); 2020 $250,000 (R22-066). Pledge $2M over 7 years; PCH 143 beds, a little over $30M (mayor, 2019-10-01 0:00:05).
reasons: partner-money: Partnerships with private donors, the foundation and the province let city dollars go further. (Earl Funk)
notes: Smaller health-related grants in the same summaries: KidSport $200 (2017) and $300 (2019), Eden Foundation $200 (2017), Haven Group $300 (2017, 2019, 2020).

title: Southeast Event Centre agreement: $10M city capital plus about $500,000 a year toward operations
summary: Council signed a memorandum of understanding with Southeast Event Centre Inc. for a $42.5M downtown arena and event centre (2,500 seats, later a 500-seat hall and gym) to replace the 1967 Centennial Arena: the city gives $10M and land and up to 0.5 mills (~$500,000) a year toward core operating costs, SEC raises at least $15M privately, and $17.5M is sought from senior governments.
status_detail: MOU approved (R19-193) and ICIP grant application filed (R19-198), both unanimous. The project depended on federal-provincial funding; the event centre opened in March 2025 (per the existing 2022–2026 report).
figures: Total $42.5M ($42,491,093 in R19-198); city $10M capital + up to 0.5 mills operating (~$500,000/yr); SEC ≥$15M; senior governments $17.5M (2019-10-01 transcript 0:29:08, 0:33:01, 0:51:37).
reasons: partner-money: For a $10M city contribution the city gets a $42.5M facility. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: City contribution capped at what it can 'reasonably afford'. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: SEC representatives presented the plan.

title: COVID-19 arrives: meetings made flexible, a day of prayer, facilities closed and budget items deferred
summary: At the March 17, 2020 meeting council recessed every 10 minutes to follow provincial distancing advice, let the mayor change or cancel April meetings on 72 hours' notice (R20-065), and agreed by consensus to Councillor Susan Penner's call for a community day of prayer on March 22. The pool and other public facilities closed in mid-March. The 2020 budget (13.7 mills, down 2.8%) was adopted April 7 with a warning that items could be deferred.
status_detail: R20-065 carried unanimously; day of prayer by consensus; 2020 Financial Plan adopted April 7, 2020 (minutes say some items may be deferred because of the pandemic).

title: Council presses the province to lift COVID-19 restrictions, citing mental health, faith and the economy
summary: From April 2020 councillors used opening remarks to question restrictions, and in June the mayor wrote to Premier Pallister urging a faster, full reopening and full-capacity church services, arguing faith gatherings are 'integral to the mental and physical health of Manitobans'. Councillors backed the letter, citing low case counts and the social, mental-health and economic toll of restrictions. By December the mayor said shutdowns were pushing many residents 'to their absolute end'.
status_detail: Letter sent June 15, 2020 and read into the record June 16 (minutes item 14); no provincial reply was reported to council. Not a recorded vote.
figures: '5 active cases' in Manitoba cited by a councillor on 2020-06-16; 1 COVID patient in hospital on 2020-05-19 (Zwaagstra opening).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Public health rules are provincial; the city's role is to voice residents' views and push for reopening. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Speaker labels I and N on 2020-06-16 are attributed as probable only (two Councillors Penner). The Nov 2020 'event that was held on Saturday' mentioned by the mayor (2020-11-17) is not named in the transcript.

title: STARS asks again for an annual contribution; referred to study session, then a 2021 grant
summary: In Sept 2020 STARS told council its provincial contract expires in 2022 and asked for an annual city contribution. Councillor Siemens asked that it go to the fall study session, and council agreed. In Nov 2020 the mayor reported STARS had flown to Steinbach 9 times in 11 days to move COVID-19 patients to hospitals with room.
status_detail: Consensus to add STARS to the Fall Study Session (minutes item 23.1). The 2021 grants summary (R22-066, approved Mar 2022) lists 'STARS Foundation 15,829.00' for 2021, the first STARS grant found.
figures: STARS Foundation $15,829 in 2021 (2022-03-15 minutes R22-066); 9 STARS trips to Steinbach in 11 days for COVID patients (mayor, 2020-11-17 1:20:42).
reasons: study-first: Asked that the request be considered at the fall study session (unrecorded). (Jac Siemens)
public: D.B. (STARS communications) presented; the 2020-09-15 meeting has no transcript.
notes: 2020-09-15 video failed to download, so the delegation and the referral come from the minutes only.

title: COVID-19 visitation shelters approved at three personal care homes
summary: Under a provincial program, PCL Constructors applied to place converted shipping-container visitation shelters at Rest Haven (two sites) and the Bethesda personal care home so residents could see family indoors over winter. A neighbour questioned the use of shipping containers and the lack of an end date; council approved all three conditional uses unanimously.
status_detail: CU-2020-05, -06 and -07 approved (R20-194, R20-195, R20-196). Province expected the shelters to open in November 2020.
figures: 103 shelters province-wide (mayor, 2020-10-20 0:25:38).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: A provincial directive implemented by Southern Health; council should facilitate it. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: T.M., a neighbour, supported visits but objected to how the shelters fit the zoning bylaw ('I love the goal. I question the execution and the plan.').

title: Mayor visits the Bethesda ER and thanks health-care workers during the second wave
summary: After a contentious weekend event that drew many emails from concerned residents, Mayor Funk told council he had joined the MLA to deliver $5,000 raised for Bethesda ER staff, saw 'firsthand' what ER workers face because of COVID-19, and thanked staff in care homes, home care and the hospital, along with STARS, the RCMP and firefighters.
status_detail: Statement under other business; no motion.
figures: $5,000 raised by the MLA for health-care workers (mayor, 2020-11-17 1:20:42).
notes: The weekend event is not named in the transcript; news reports describe an anti-restriction rally in Steinbach on Nov 14, 2020 (not verified from council sources).

title: Councillor's opening opposes expanded assisted dying and calls for palliative care
summary: In the Nov 17, 2020 opening, a Councillor Penner criticized federal Bill C-7 (expanding medical assistance in dying) and asked where the political will was to give all Canadians quality palliative care.
status_detail: Opening remarks only; no motion or letter recorded.
figures: 'Only 30% of Canadians have access to quality palliative care' (as stated in the opening).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Framed as federal legislation and national palliative-care policy. (Councillor Penner)

title: Clearspring Greens pathway rebuilt as a cheaper plan and completed in 2021
summary: A 2020 plan for an asphalt pathway linking the Clearspring Greens neighbourhood to the Aquatic Centre and the city's path network drew 78 objections from 146 parcels. In January 2021 Councillor Susan Penner moved to cancel it and start over without lights, splitting the asphalt cost 50/50 with residents up to $1,610 per parcel (the city's sidewalk fee on new lots). The new plan drew only a handful of objections, was approved by the Municipal Board, built in 2021 and financed by a smaller-than-planned debenture.
status_detail: Old plan cancelled and new plan ordered (R21-011, R21-012, Jan 5); by-law 2168 first and second readings (R21-032/033, Feb 16), third reading after Municipal Board approval (R21-076, Apr 20); built in the 2021 capital works tender (R21-077); debenture by-law 2195 (R21-276/277, R22-046), all unanimous. Councillors said in Feb 2022 that the path is heavily used.
figures: Project about $650,000; borrowing authorized $233,450, actually $136,850 at 2.42% after 60 owners prepaid (transcripts Feb 16, 2021 0:09:21; Feb 15, 2022 0:36:18). Old plan about $4,200 then $2,850 per parcel; lights $160,000 dropped; new cap $1,610 per parcel (transcript Jan 5, 2021). 78 objections to the old plan; 7 written (6 remaining) to the new one.
reasons: cost: Dropped the lights and capped residents' share at the $1,610 sidewalk fee so the neighbourhood would accept it. (Susan Penner); fairness-precedent: $1,610 is what every new-lot buyer has paid for sidewalks for 14 years, so it is fair and 'sellable'. (Jac Siemens)
public: One objector (initials withheld) at the Feb 16, 2021 hearing withdrew after hearing the lower cost. Siemens recounted a boy (unnamed) who could only reach the pump track by being driven.
seconder: Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert
notes: Framed by council mainly as pedestrian safety; included here as active transportation.

title: Requests from Katie Cares and Ronald McDonald House received as information, not funded
summary: Katie Cares (Katie's Cottage, respite for children with complex medical needs) asked for grants in January and December 2021, and Ronald McDonald House Charities Manitoba (housing for families of children in hospital) in February and December 2021 and December 2022. Each was received as information without discussion. A Katie Cares delegation booked for Aug 3, 2021 did not attend.
status_detail: Never refused by vote, but neither charity appears in the 2020, 2021 or 2022 grant summaries (R22-066, R23-039), so no grant was paid.
notes: 'refunding' is as transcribed (probably 'a funding request').

title: Pat Porter Active Living Centre asks for help with fundraising and a heating/cooling system
summary: The seniors' active living centre (run by Serving Seniors Inc.) sent a 2021 fundraising request in January and, in October 2021, a grant request for its heating and cooling system. Both were received as information; the mayor sent the October request to the fall study session.
status_detail: No decision at a recorded meeting. The grant summaries show Serving Seniors received $10,000 in 2020 and $500 in 2021 (R22-066), and only the transit contract in 2022 (R23-039), so no heating/cooling grant is visible for 2021–2022.
figures: Serving Seniors grants: $10,000 (2020), $500 (2021) (minutes R22-066, column positions checked in the PDF).
reasons: study-first: Sent the request to the fall study session. (Mayor Earl Funk)
notes: The amount requested was not stated at the meeting.

title: New care homes welcomed; assisted-living site approved; councillor urges palliative care
summary: Council approved a conditional use for Silver Lining Care's assisted-living cottages on Beaver Crescent (July 2021: two buildings of 10 units for people needing home care). The Cottages opened in late April 2022 and the new 143-suite Rest Haven personal care home, built by the Haven Group with the Bethesda Foundation, opened in May 2022. Councillors marked both in opening remarks; in August 2022 Councillor Susan Penner used her opening to argue for wider access to palliative care rather than medical assistance in dying.
status_detail: CU-2021-03 approved unanimously (R21-141, July 6, 2021; minutes only, video unavailable). Both facilities opened in spring 2022. Palliative-care remarks were a personal statement; no council motion followed.
figures: Rest Haven: 143 suites; Haven Group and Bethesda Foundation raised $6.55M, 'just under 20% of total cost' (Bill Hiebert, May 4, 2021). Silver Lining: 2 buildings x 10 units (minutes July 6, 2021). Penner: 'only 30% of Canadians' have access to palliative care (Aug 16, 2022; not verified).
public: Two neighbours wrote with concerns about the Beaver Crescent assisted-living site; no one spoke at the hearing (minutes July 6, 2021).
notes: The July 6, 2021 meeting video could not be downloaded, so the approval comes from the minutes only. Penner's Aug 2022 remarks also criticized MAiD policy; that part is outside council's powers.

title: Southeast Event Centre approved: arena, gym courts and walking track; city share grows from $10M to about $23M
summary: Council moved the Southeast Event Centre (replacing the 1960s Centennial Arena) from funding to construction: $1.2M more into the Recreation Reserve (May 2021), design contract (Sept 2021), a $7.5M local-improvement borrowing by-law (Dec 2021–Apr 2022), $1.4M of land from the Recreation Reserve (Apr 2022) and, in Nov 2022, a $61M construction contract with $13.2M more city money. Members described a 2,500-seat arena plus gym courts for pickleball and volleyball and an indoor walking track that downtown seniors could walk to.
status_detail: All readings and contracts carried unanimously (R21-199, R21-204, R21-249, R22-100, R22-103, R22-254, R22-255). Completion was then expected in fall 2024; the centre opened in March 2025 (2022–2026 report).
figures: Dec 2021: total about $42.5M = ICIP grant ~$17.5M + private $15M + city $10M ($7.5M borrowed over 5 years at ~1.53 mills, about $138 a year on a $200,000 home, + $2.5M reserves) (transcript Dec 7, 2021 0:06:16). Design contract $1,898,430 (R21-199). Land $1.4M from Recreation Reserve (R22-103). Nov 2022: lowest bid $75.3M cut to a $61M guaranteed maximum price (R22-254); private pledge raised to $25.5M; extra city funds $11.4M reserves + $1.785M operating, plus up to $5M more debt if needed (R22-255); city share about $23M (Susan Penner, transcript Nov 1, 2022 1:46:17).
reasons: partner-money: City taxpayers pay 'less than a quarter' (2021) because private donors and other governments fund a bigger, multi-use building. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: Costs rose with COVID, but saying no would mean losing partners' money and paying more later. (Susan Penner)
public: Seven letters were received for the Dec 7, 2021 hearing; some questioned the size (2,500 seats), per Zwaagstra. No one spoke at the hearing.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R21-199, R22-100, R22-103, R22-254, R22-255); Susan Penner (R21-204); Jac Siemens (R21-249)
seconder: Jac Siemens; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner
notes: Included because the 2022–2026 report treats the event centre as council's main healthy-living investment; council itself framed it mostly as an arena and community venue.

title: STARS air ambulance funded at $1 per resident a year ($15,829)
summary: Council had agreed (in 2020, per STARS) to give the STARS air ambulance foundation $1 per resident a year for the rest of the 2018–2022 term. The 2021 payment was made in July 2021 and STARS' thank-you letter was received in August; council's grant summaries show $15,829 paid in both 2021 and 2022.
status_detail: Paid in 2021 and 2022 ($15,829 each year, grant summaries R22-066 and R23-039). The original commitment was made before this period (STARS' delegate on Sept 20, 2022 said council decided it '2 years ago').
figures: $15,829 a year = $1 x 15,829 residents (2016 census population) (minutes R22-066 for 2021; R23-039, Feb 21, 2023, for 2022).
public: STARS (Manitoba) thanked council by letter (Aug 17, 2021, received as information).
notes: The 2020 council decision itself is outside this period and was not checked here.

title: City joins a regional cost-shared review of the Vivian silica sand mine to protect drinking water
summary: With six other southeastern municipalities, council agreed to share the cost of an independent review (legal, engineering) of the proposed silica sand mine near Vivian, including its possible effects on the aquifer the region drinks from. The mayor and city manager were named to the regional committee.
status_detail: Resolution R21-194 carried unanimously. No results of the review were reported at a recorded council meeting in 2021–2022.
figures: 7 municipalities (transcript 0:55:29); cost share not stated.
reasons: partner-money: Cost-sharing with neighbours who 'share the same concerns' about drinking water. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Province announces $32M Bethesda expansion with dialysis and 23 beds; council welcomes it
summary: In October 2021 the province announced an expansion of Bethesda Regional Health Centre: 23 acute-care beds, a six-station kidney dialysis unit and upgraded chemotherapy as a regional cancer hub. Councillors celebrated it in opening remarks; no council resolution or recorded advocacy for it was found in 2021–2022 meetings. Council's own role came later, when it rezoned land for the expansion (see 2022-hospital-street-rezoning).
status_detail: Announced and paid for by the province; the expansion opened to patients in March 2026 (existing 2022–2026 report).
figures: $32M expansion, 23 acute beds, 6 dialysis stations (Bill Hiebert, transcript Dec 7, 2021, 0:00:08). Steinbach has 'pretty close to 200 beds' and 'more than 50 doctors' (same remarks; not independently verified).
notes: The transcript spells the premier 'Gertsen' (Kelvin Goertzen). Bill Hiebert repeated the expansion in his July 5, 2022 re-election remarks.

title: Handi-Transit handed to Serving Seniors under a city funding agreement
summary: After a study-session discussion, staff proposed paying a local non-profit to run the city's Handi-Transit service for people with mobility needs. Council approved the Steinbach Accessible Transportation Services Agreement with Serving Seniors Inc. (which runs the Pat Porter Active Living Centre) in December 2021, with service starting in early 2022 at about the same cost to the city.
status_detail: Agreement approved unanimously (R21-253). The 2022 grant summary shows $102,921.49 paid to 'Serving Seniors - Transit' (R23-039, Feb 21, 2023).
figures: $102,921.49 to Serving Seniors for transit in 2022 (minutes R23-039). Handi-Transit financial report for 2020 accepted July 20, 2021 (R21-162).
reasons: cost: Proceed only if the service could be delivered 'without a significant change in cost'. (Council (study-session direction, as reported by staff))
notes: Staff's remark that council wanted no significant cost change sits in a turn the diarization split between speakers; paraphrased, not quoted.

title: Council asks the Premier to repeal all COVID-19 public health restrictions
summary: After the mayor's opening remarks on his 'COVID journey', council agreed by consensus on Feb 1, 2022 that he write to Premier Heather Stefanson thanking the province for the vaccination campaign, agreeing with a 'balanced approach' to living with the virus, and asking it to repeal all health restrictions. The mayor encouraged everyone eligible to get vaccinated. Several councillors had argued in opening remarks, before and after, that restrictions and vaccine mandates had gone on too long.
status_detail: Letter authorized by consensus (minutes Feb 1, 2022, item 12.1). Two weeks later Zwaagstra noted the province had announced virtually all restrictions would end by mid-March 2022.
figures: Mayor cited an Angus Reid poll (32% strongly agree restrictions should end, 16% strongly disagree) and about 90% of Canadian adults double vaccinated (transcript 0:02:46, 0:15:55).
reasons: restrictions-harm: Businesses 'can't thrive at 50%'; people are weary; time to live with COVID while protecting the vulnerable. (Mayor Earl Funk); restrictions-harm: About 90% of eligible Canadians vaccinated; restrictions have a 'profoundly negative impact the longer that they go on'. (Michael Zwaagstra); restrictions-harm: Asked whether COVID still requires emergency health orders and whether 'the cure' is worse than the disease (Jan 18 opening). (Susan Penner)
notes: Zwaagstra's Feb 15, 2022 opening also urged patience with people who were more 'COVID-cautious'. Turns by an unresolved Hiebert (0:12:33) and an unidentified councillor (0:11:45, 0:15:22) also supported the letter but are not attributed. The letter itself was not found.

title: City grants $250,000 a year to the Bethesda Foundation (2020–2022)
summary: The city's annual grant summaries show $250,000 a year to the Bethesda Foundation, the charity that raises money for Bethesda Regional Health Centre and related facilities, in 2020, 2021 and 2022. The grants were accepted as part of routine grant-summary resolutions; no council debate about them was found in 2021–2022.
status_detail: Paid each year (R22-066 for 2020 and 2021; R23-039 for 2022). The original commitment and its purpose were not stated in 2021–2022 meetings.
notes: What the $250,000 a year is for (e.g., a pledge toward a specific project) was not stated in this period; check the 2018–2020 records.

title: Mayor backs Adult & Teen Challenge addiction-recovery residence; its tax-relief request received as information
summary: The mayor said he had supported bringing an Adult & Teen Challenge chapter (a faith-based addiction recovery program) to Steinbach since early in his term; its residence opened in May 2022 in a building donated by a local church. In November 2022 the organization asked the city for a property-tax reduction or exemption for its 73 Westview Drive property; council received the request as information with no recorded decision.
status_detail: Tax relief request received as information Nov 15, 2022 (minutes item 21); no decision found in 2022. The mayor's support was personal and practical (he cooked for the opening); no city funding was recorded.
public: A local parent (M.P.) whose son completed the program asked the mayor early in his term to help bring the program to Steinbach (as told by the mayor).
notes: The tax-exemption request should be followed into 2023.

title: RCMP concern about home cannabis grows referred to staff for a zoning review
summary: With the yearly RCMP priorities (which include D.A.R.E. drug-resistance classes for grades 6 and 8), council received a letter from the RCMP about cannabis grown in homes, including under Health Canada medical licences. Zwaagstra noted medical licences are outside city jurisdiction but suggested staff look at whether the zoning bylaw could set limits; council agreed by consensus to ask for a report.
status_detail: Referred to administration for a report; no report or bylaw change on home cannabis grows was found at a recorded meeting in 2022 or 2023.
reasons: not-council-role: Medical cannabis licences come from Health Canada and are 'outside of the city's jurisdiction'; only zoning limits might be possible. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: The minutes for May 17, 2022 were not checked for a separate item on the RCMP letter; the referral is taken from the transcript.

title: Hospital Street lots rezoned for Bethesda's expansion (By-law 2214)
summary: Southern Health asked council to rezone three homes at 417, 425 and 431 Hospital Street from residential to educational/institutional so it could buy them for the hospital's long-term growth, starting with relocated parking. Council gave first reading in August and second and third readings after a public hearing in September 2022, with no objections.
status_detail: By-law 2214 passed unanimously (R22-186 first reading Aug 2; R22-206/207 second and third readings Sept 6, 2022). No written correspondence or objectors at the hearing.
figures: 3 lots, RLD to E/I (minutes Sept 6, 2022).
public: Southern Health's regional facilities manager R.P. said the purchase depended on the rezoning and was part of a long-term plan to move the hospital toward Loewen Boulevard; the owners supported it (per Zwaagstra).
notes: A further supporting comment at 1:31:47 came from a Councillor Hiebert whom the speaker map cannot resolve (low), so it is not attributed.

title: STARS asks for $1.50 per resident a year for 2022–2026; referred to a closed study session
summary: STARS' Manitoba representative asked council to raise its support from $1 to $1.50 per resident a year for the new four-year term, saying Steinbach received more STARS missions than almost any other Manitoba community and that air transfers keep Bethesda's ER doctor and nurse in town. Councillors asked about other municipalities' support and STARS' budget; the mayor referred the request to a study session.
status_detail: Referred to the (unrecorded) study session. No decision on the $1.50 rate appears in the 2022 minutes; the 2022 grant summary still shows $15,829 ($1 per resident).
figures: Request $1.50 per resident a year for 4 years (transcript 0:13:29; minutes item 6.2). 317 STARS missions to Steinbach in 10 years; 54 in the last fiscal year; ground transfers take a local doctor and nurse out of the ER for about 4 hours; STARS budget about $13M, 80–85% provincial, about $3M raised yearly (transcript 0:10:58–0:17:24).
reasons: study-first: Took the request to council's study session rather than deciding at the meeting. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: STARS delegate D.B. said 'well over half' of municipalities in STARS' catchment support it, many at $1 per resident and some at $2.
notes: A question at 0:17:15 on STARS' budget came from 'Councillor Pinner' (speaker map: Susan Penner, medium confidence), so it is not attributed by name. The outcome of the request should be checked in the 2023 grant summary (2023 period).

title: Council endorses swim club's $25,000 provincial grant bid for Aquatic Centre starting blocks
summary: As owner of the Aquatic Centre, the city had to approve the Steinbach Skimmers swim club's application to Manitoba's Arts, Culture and Sport in Community Fund for six removable starting blocks. Council passed the resolution of support unanimously; no city money was involved.
status_detail: Support resolution R22-232 carried unanimously; the grant's outcome was not reported to council in 2022.
figures: $25,000 provincial grant sought for 6 starting blocks (minutes R22-232).
notes: A councillor Hiebert added 'we want to promote healthy living' (0:41:46), but the speaker map merges the two Hieberts (low), so it is not attributed.

title: Chamber reports attending a rural doctor recruitment summit; doctor recruitment raised at the election forum
summary: In its annual presentation the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce told council it had attended the Rural Physician Recruitment and Retention Summit in Portage la Prairie, and noted that Councillor Siemens had raised doctor recruitment at the October 2022 election forum. Council asked no questions about doctors and took no action. This is the only mention of doctor recruitment found in 2021–2022 council meetings.
status_detail: No council action in 2022. The city's first recruitment steps came later (residents' retreat 2023, Mayor's Doctor Recruitment Task Force 2024; see the 2022–2026 report).
public: Chamber chair C.B. presented; the Chamber's director and a local business owner attended the summit (names withheld).
notes: Siemens' election-forum remark is reported second-hand by the delegate; the forum itself was not reviewed.

title: Children's recreation charity allowed occasional book sales in the industrial park (5–2)
summary: ROC Eastman (Recreation Opportunities for Children), which helps low-income families get children into sports, wanted to hold book-sale fundraisers up to four times a year in a warehouse unit at 110 Industrial Road. Council approved a conditional use limited to ROC Eastman and two units. The two votes against were about keeping retail out of light-industrial zones, not about the charity.
status_detail: CU-2022-04 approved 5–2 (R22-262), subject to a major occupancy agreement.
figures: Up to 4 sales a year; 2 units of about 1,200 sq ft each; 6 parking stalls (transcript 0:21:42–0:30:24).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Voted against: the area is zoned light industrial and retail should not creep in. (Jake Hiebert); fairness-precedent: Voted against: conditions not specific enough; the use could change. (Damian Penner)
public: ROC Eastman's executive director M.L. said the charity could not run more than four sales a year.
notes: Included as the only divided vote touching recreation in the period; the dispute was land use.

title: Recreation operating budget $4.6M (2023) and $4.8M (2024); pool called a quality-of-life piece
summary: The 2023 and 2024 financial plans funded the aquatic centre, arenas, A.D. Penner Park, curling rink, soccer park and green space. Councillor Siemens repeatedly described the pool and recreation as quality-of-life services and said Steinbach needs more active-transportation routes and green space. Council also supported provincial sport-fund grant applications by the swim club and curling club.
status_detail: Both financial plans adopted unanimously (R23-053, R24-073). No new active-transportation projects were funded in these budgets.
figures: Recreation facilities operating $4.6M (2023), $4.8M (2024) (financial plan presentations, transcripts 2023-03-21 0:12:14, 2024-04-02 0:05:52). Aquatic centre ~20% (2023) and ~18% (2024) of city labour. 86,000 public swims and 42,000+ swimming lessons (Siemens, 2023-03-21 0:23:35). 2024 mill rate +5.1% to 14.4 (Zwaagstra 0:18:11). Swim club timing grant support $25,000 (R23-087) and curling club $17,242 (R23-088).
reasons: cost: Toughest budget; renewal projects spread into future years. (Jac Siemens)

title: Southeast Event Centre: cost rises to $69.2M; city share about $30M
summary: Council proceeded with the Southeast Event Centre (arena, gym, walking track and community space) through 2023-2024. It passed the local improvement plan borrowing by-law in 2023, approved $8.5M more funding and an $8.153M change order in December 2023 when costs rose to $69.153M, and gave first and second reading to a $7.5M debt by-law in December 2024. A provincial Safe Healthy Communities grant of up to $50,000 was conditionally approved for a play zone.
status_detail: All funding votes unanimous; construction continued and the centre opened in March 2025.
figures: Total $69.153M (transcript 2023-12-19 0:32:15); city share "just over $30 million" (Siemens 0:36:13). Extra $8.5M: operating fund $1.55M, new provincial grant $3.6M, L&B reserve $0.85M, debt $2.5M (R23-252). Change order $8.153M (R23-253). Debt by-law 2256 $7.5M (R24-255/256). Play Zone grant up to $50,000 (minutes Nov 5, 2024 item 26).
reasons: cost: Construction inflation and soil/mechanical redesign raised costs; contingency borrowing had been pre-approved. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner
seconder: Susan Penner; Damian Penner; Damian Penner; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Bill Hiebert
notes: The event centre spans several topics (taxes-spending covers its finances in detail).

title: Councillor Zwaagstra: government should do fewer things and focus on essentials
summary: In meeting openings, Councillor Zwaagstra argued that government works best when it does fewer things, suggesting money for a new federal dental program would be better spent on surgical wait times, and later that safe drinking water and basic infrastructure are municipal essentials that come before other initiatives.
status_detail: Statements of philosophy; no motion.
reasons: not-council-role: "government works best when it does fewer things, not more things." (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Existing published report cites the 2023-05-02 quote at 0:01:58; the turn begins at 0:00:14.

title: Hospital-area parking: letter asks Southern Health staff to use staff lots
summary: After a resident's letter about parking near Bethesda during the hospital and event-centre construction, staff met hospital management and canvassed residents. Council extended 2-hour parking on Henry Street, planned 2-hour zones on Hospital Street after construction, and wrote to Southern Health and Bethesda asking staff to park in designated lots.
status_detail: Report accepted with options 1 and 4 (R23-196), unanimous.
public: A resident of Ash Avenue wrote to council (May 2023); residents were canvassed door to door.
notes: Minor access item; included because it is the only recorded council correspondence with Southern Health on the hospital in 2023-2024.

title: Council sponsors AMM resolution against ambulance "lift-assist" calls going to firefighters
summary: The mayor said paid-on-call firefighters were increasingly called to help paramedics lift patients, from 1-3 calls a year to a possible 40-60 in 2023. Council sponsored an AMM cities-caucus resolution asking the province to end the practice of downloading EMS lift assists onto municipal fire departments.
status_detail: Resolution sponsored (R23-119) and sent to AMM. No report back on the province's response was found at recorded meetings in 2023-2024.
figures: Lift assists: 1-3 a year historically, "up to 40, 50, 60" projected for 2023; fire department about 300 calls a year (transcript 0:41:11, 0:44:46). Siemens: once "8 or 9 times a year" (0:43:46).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Health care being downloaded to municipalities; the province and health authority should provide it. (Michael Zwaagstra); provincial-responsibility: Lift assists are the regional health authority's and EMS workers' job. (Earl Funk)
vote: carried; no opposition heard in transcript (minutes do not record the outcome line)
notes: Existing published report cites the Zwaagstra quote at 0:42:54; the turn begins at 0:42:49.

title: Land rezoned and subdivided for future health-care facilities near the Family Medical Centre
summary: Bethesda Wellness Inc. applied to rezone part of 385 Loewen Boulevard (Steinbach Campus Foundation land) from development reserve to educational-institutional and subdivide it to allow future health-care facilities beside the Steinbach Family Medical Centre. Council gave all three readings and approved the subdivision with a Heritage Parkway extension; no one objected.
status_detail: By-law 2234 first reading R23-152 (Jul 18), second R23-164 and third R23-165 (Aug 15); subdivision R23-177 (Sept 5), all unanimous. What will be built was not stated.
figures: Three new parcels and two public reserve parcels (transcript 2023-09-05 0:06:35). Land originally about 60 acres donated for institutional, health and educational use (Siemens, 2023-08-15 0:07:00).
public: Applicant J.K. (for Bethesda Wellness Inc.) attended the Sept 5 hearing; no objections.
mover: Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Bill Hiebert; Bill Hiebert
notes: Applicant named in minutes; shown by initials here.

title: Up to $10,000 to host the 2023 family-medicine residents' retreat
summary: Southern Health-Santé Sud asked the city to take part in physician-recruitment events. The mayor proposed picking one and doing it well: the provincial Family Medicine Resident Retreat in Steinbach on Sept 22-24, 2023. Council authorized up to $10,000 from the 2023 surplus for events and promotions during the retreat.
status_detail: Funding authorized unanimously (R23-153). How much was spent and what the residents were shown was not reported at a recorded council meeting in 2023-2024.
figures: Up to $10,000 from 2023 surplus (minutes R23-153). Siemens: "7,000, 8,000" Steinbach-area people looking for a doctor per Find a Doc Manitoba (transcript 0:54:00).
reasons: targeted-only: Supported it because it targeted something specific: all Manitoba family-medicine residents in Steinbach at the point they choose where to practise. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Request came by letter from Southern Health-Santé Sud (an organization).
notes: A mis-heard rendering of the city's name was trimmed from the Siemens quote with an ellipsis.

title: STARS air ambulance: city keeps paying $1 per resident a year
summary: STARS presented to council in September 2023 and September 2024, thanking the city for its $1-per-capita annual contribution. Councillors asked about how many municipalities contribute and how STARS is funded. A November 2024 STARS letter asking for $1-$2 per capita was received as information.
status_detail: The $1-per-capita contribution continued ($17,806 donation acknowledged Nov 7, 2023). The Nov 2024 suggestion of up to $2 per capita was received as information with no recorded increase.
figures: 2022 grant $15,829 (R23-039); 2023 donation $17,806 (minutes Nov 7, 2023 item 16); over $49,000 since 2019 (STARS, Sept 3, 2024, transcript 0:07:16). Missions: 92 to Steinbach and area in 2022-23 (39 to the city); 38 + 41 in 2023-24 (transcripts). STARS raises about 20% (~$3M/yr) by fundraising (minutes Sept 19, 2023).
public: D.B. (2023) and A.C. (2024), STARS development staff, presented; STARS is an organization.
notes: The Sept 19, 2023 transcript puts a STARS director's answer (0:20:18) under the mayor's letter; it is not used.

title: Bethesda expansion under way; mayor notes Steinbach left out of provincial hospital plans
summary: A $44M building permit for the Bethesda Regional Health Centre addition was issued in 2023. After the new government's November 2023 throne speech, the mayor said he was concerned it named hospital expansions in Winnipeg and Brandon but not Steinbach, and asked how council would advocate for the region.
status_detail: No council resolution or letter on provincial hospital priorities followed in 2023-2024. The expansion itself is provincially funded and opened in 2026.
figures: Hospital addition building permit $44 million (transcript 2023-09-19 0:08:11).

title: Helipad at Bethesda raised with STARS, not pursued
summary: With the $44M Bethesda expansion under way, Councillor Siemens asked STARS whether it could push for a helipad at the hospital. STARS said the request has to come from the community, that a pad would cut about 20 minutes from transfers, and that it would welcome someone to advocate for one.
status_detail: No council motion, letter or follow-up on a helipad was recorded in 2023-2024.
figures: Base-to-airport flight 16-17 minutes plus about 30 minutes by ambulance to and from the hospital (STARS, transcript 0:23:01).
public: D.B. (STARS) said St. Anne's community built its pad and a benefactor paid for Boundary Trails'; a Steinbach pad would cost more; STARS had spoken to the Bethesda Foundation.
